first.rationale: The measured problems are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and two independent inherited records (memory_86 on shortening onboarding, memory_31 on signup field reduction) point at the same lever, with onboarding sitting upstream of activation so a single fix can plausibly move both. I am deliberately not chasing the competitor with promotional_pricing: memory_73 shows acquisition/revenue lift but a material 30-day retention hit and carries an explicit warning against generalizing it, which conflicts directly with the sustainable long-term qualified revenue objective. Referral incentives (memory_57) target established customers and do not address the funnel decline that is actually degrading; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a real signal but is a different segment from the SMB pressure and the observed declines. I am spending both verification pulls on the two memories I intend to act on rather than on the one I am declining, because memory_73 already carries its own caveat and does not change my choice. memory_31 is day 12 and the oldest record here, so staleness matters; memory_86 is a consolidated summary whose original segment breakdown and effect size I want to see before sizing the change. Key downstream risk to flag: cutting required signup fields can strip the firmographic data used for lead qualification and routing, so raw activation could rise while qualified revenue falls, and per memory_44 any simplification must not divert enterprise prospects off the demo-request path. I will therefore instrument the test on qualified-pipeline quality and 30-day retention, not just completion and activation, and treat the two supporting memories as correlated evidence for one lever rather than two independent confirmations.

final.rationale: Verification changed the shape of the decision without changing the lever. The consolidated memory_86 ('shortening onboarding improved completion and time-to-value') had silently dropped the source record's central caveat: 60-day churn +9% concentrated in complex-workspace accounts, with an explicit instruction not to roll out there. memory_31 verified cleanly but only as narrowly as it was stated: SMB signup +15%, activation +9%, qualified revenue +4%, with a small 30-day retention cost of -1%, and explicitly not replicated outside SMB. So the durable-memory summaries were directionally right but caveat-stripped in one case and segment-bound in the other; that is itself evidence to treat the remaining unverified summaries (memory_91, memory_57, memory_44) as similarly lossy. I still run simplify_onboarding, because it is the only lever with a verified positive qualified-revenue effect and it sits upstream of both declining metrics. But I scope it hard rather than running it broadly: SMB self-serve, simple-workspace accounts only; complex-workspace accounts explicitly excluded per exp_86; enterprise prospects left on the demo-request path per memory_44, which I did not verify and am treating as unconfirmed but not worth overriding. I hold to declining promotional_pricing despite direct competitive pressure on exactly the price-sensitive SMB segment being attacked, since memory_73's retention harm runs against the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective and the short-term acquisition win would be borrowed from later churn. Downstream risks I am instrumenting rather than assuming away: removing signup fields can strip firmographic data used for qualification and routing, so raw activation can rise while qualified revenue falls; and the -1% retention and +9% complex-account churn are both real, so I gate on 30-day retention and 60-day churn by workspace complexity, not just completion and activation. Kill criteria set in advance on those gates. Residual uncertainty: exp_86 and exp_31 are partly the same lever measured twice, so they are correlated evidence, not independent confirmation, and neither was run under active competitive price pressure, which may compress the effect.
